I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette:
David is a 63-year-old rabbi who came to therapy at his wife’s quiet but persistent urging. For the past several months, she had watched him shrink. He avoided the weekly oneg Shabbat, the social hour after services, claiming fatigue. He snapped at congregants who approached him too quickly from behind. At home, he sat at the dining table with his back to the wall and flinched when she touched his shoulder to wake him. She had stopped touching him. He was grateful for that, and ashamed of his gratitude.

The event that had shaped his life happened more than thirty years ago, when David was a young man in a city that no longer felt safe. He and his family were Jewish, and the state had turned against them. One night, armed men broke into their apartment. David remembered the shouting—the raw, triumphant bellowing of men who enjoyed terror. He remembered being grabbed by the collar and thrown against a wall, a rifle butt pressed into his throat, the cold metal of a knife blade drawn across his cheek as a taunt. He had screamed for his father, but his father was already on the floor, and his mother was being pulled into the bedroom. David had frozen. He had not fought. He had not saved them. He had been pulled out of the building by a neighbor and smuggled across a border. He learned later that his parents had not survived. The last time he saw them, he was being shoved out the door, his mother’s shouting suddenly cut off.

In the years after, David built a life. He studied, he married a kind woman, he became a rabbi. He told himself that God had spared him for a reason. But the reason never felt earned. He had come to believe, deep and wordless, that he deserved to suffer. The punishment thinking was not a conscious decision—it was a quiet voice that said *you let them die, so you don’t get to feel safe now*. When his heart raced in a quiet room, when he sweated through a sermon, he told himself this was simply what he owed. He did not deserve to be touched with gentleness. He did not deserve his wife’s patience.

His work as a rabbi once felt like a calling; now it felt like a minefield. The synagogue was full of triggers he could not prepare for. A child running up behind him and grabbing his hand sent him into a cold sweat, his body reacting as if he were still in that apartment. A congregant raising his voice during a heated discussion about the Torah portion—even in good faith—made David’s vision tunnel and his throat close. He had learned to scan every room for objects that could be used as weapons: the silver Kiddush cup, the long shofar, even the heavy prayer book. He catalogued them without meaning to, and then he chose his seat carefully, always near an exit, always with a wall behind him, never with his back to the door. There were only two places he felt even close to safe: the small study in his home and the empty sanctuary late at night, when no one else was there.

His concentration had frayed. During sermons, he lost his train of thought mid-sentence. He had started writing out every word of his weekly talk, but even then he stumbled. He could not rely on his own mind; he could not rely on his own body. The body was an enemy that kept flooding him with adrenaline when he was perfectly safe. And he knew, with a certainty that felt real, that someone else—a stronger man, a more decisive man—would have stopped the event. He would have fought back. He would have saved his parents. David had not. So who was he to trust himself now?

To cope, he had developed routines that he did not see as strategies so much as survival. He kept himself busy—too busy to think. He took on extra committee meetings, visited the sick, wrote long emails. At home, he distracted himself with the television or a book until his eyes burned and he could collapse into bed. But the deepest avoidance was intimacy. He loved his wife, but he could not let her close. To be emotionally close meant to risk being seen, and to be seen meant she would discover the cowardice he carried. He had stopped confiding in her. He had stopped reaching for her in bed. She had begun to cry during their arguments about his distance, and he had sat there, frozen, unable to comfort her, hating himself for it.

What finally brought David to seek help was not his own desire but a specific moment in the synagogue. A bar mitzvah boy had stumbled over a blessing, and the boy’s father—a well-meaning man—raised his voice sharply in correction. David had flinched so visibly that several congregants noticed. He had excused himself to his office and sat shaking for ten minutes. His wife found him there. She did not say she told him so. She simply said, “David, you need someone to talk to.” He did not believe talking would change anything. He was certain the past would always be inside him, waiting. But he was also afraid—afraid that if he did not change, he would lose his marriage, his congregation, and the last thread of meaning in his life. He came to the first session with his hands clasped tight on his knees, sitting in the last chair in the room, the one with the wall behind it. He said, “I don’t know if this can help. But I cannot keep living this way.”
